# Bone & joint health

> *The ageing musculoskeleton prompts some of the most common questions a doctor hears: "What should I eat?"
> and "Should I take a supplement?" Bone responds to real, correctable dietary factors, while osteoarthritis and
> gout have almost the mirror-image story: their main treatment is weight loss (or, for gout, a drug), and
> their best-selling supplement does not work.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Distinguish osteoporosis, osteoarthritis and gout, and match each to its main nutrition-related measure (calcium, vitamin D and protein for osteoporosis, weight loss for osteoarthritis, a urate-lowering drug for gout).
- Explain bone as tissue in constant turnover, and why a higher peak bone mass delays osteoporosis by years.
- Explain how calcium, vitamin D and protein each act on bone, and why calcium bioavailability matters more
  than calcium content.
- Identify who benefits from calcium and vitamin D supplements, and explain why blanket supplementation of
  replete adults does not prevent fractures.
- Evaluate glucosamine and other joint-supplement claims against the guideline evidence.
- Recognise the bone red flags (low body weight, a fragility fracture) and refer using OSTA, FRAX and DXA.
:::

## Bone & joint health at a glance {#sec-bone-overview}

The two musculoskeletal questions a generalist hears most often, *"what should I take for my bones?"* and
*"should I take glucosamine for my joints?"*, concern different systems. **Osteoporosis** (low bone density,
silent until a bone breaks) is common and costly: Singapore's hip-fracture *rate* is falling, but the *count*
keeps rising with ageing [@koh2001hipfracSG; @chandran2019burdenSG]. Knee **osteoarthritis** (worn, painful
joint cartilage) and **gout** (a metabolic disease in which uric acid crystals inflame the joint) are common
too [@leung2018sgkoa; @lee2023sggout], and supplements are heavily marketed for both. For bone, calcium, vitamin D and
protein are strong, correctable factors; for the joints, the answer is usually to lose weight, skip the
supplement and refer.

Four principles apply throughout:

- Peak bone mass is reached in young adulthood (from the late teens to the thirties, depending on the skeletal site), and only about 20–40% of it is modifiable by
  lifestyle, a real but bounded influence: peak bone mass is built in youth, and the rate of later bone loss matters for
  the rest of life [@nof_weaver_2016_pbm_position].
- What counts is how much calcium is absorbed (its bioavailability), not the number on the label, and a
  multi-ethnic, partly lactose-intolerant population can meet its needs without milk
  [@weaverVegCalcium1999; @healthhubCalciumSG].
- Calcium and vitamin D help people who are genuinely short, but blanket supplements for already-replete
  community-dwelling adults do not prevent fractures [@zhao2017cavitdNoBenefit].
- For the joints, the best-marketed supplement (glucosamine) is the one the guidelines advise against; the
  effective measures are weight loss for osteoarthritis and a urate-lowering drug for gout [@wandel2010nma;
  @kolasinski2020acr].

## Three conditions people confuse {#sec-bone-conditions}

Patients, and busy clinics, often mix up osteoporosis, osteoarthritis and gout, yet the three need different
nutrition, and getting them backwards is a common error.

![Three conditions patients confuse, and their different diet stories. Osteoporosis is a bone-density problem, silent until a bone breaks in a minor fall (a fragility fracture), where nutrition genuinely helps (calcium, vitamin D, protein). Osteoarthritis is worn joint cartilage, painful, whose one effective dietary measure is weight loss; supplements don't rebuild cartilage. Gout is a urate-crystal metabolic disease where diet nudges urate only modestly and the real treatment is a urate-lowering drug.](/figures/mechanisms/bone-joint-disambiguation.svg){#fig-disambiguation width="94%" fig-align="center"}

The trap is treating them alike: calcium does nothing for arthritis, glucosamine does nothing for
osteoporosis, and gout is neither wear nor thinning.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient with knee osteoarthritis starts calcium tablets for his joints. Why won't they help?
Osteoarthritis is worn joint cartilage, not low bone density, so calcium, which acts on bone, does not act
on it. The one effective dietary measure for osteoarthritis is weight loss. Calcium belongs to osteoporosis, a
different condition with a different diet story.
:::

## Pathophysiology: bone remodelling {#sec-bone-bank}

Bone is living tissue in constant turnover, not inert scaffolding, which is why diet matters even for
something as solid as the skeleton. Two cell types do the work:

Osteoblasts
: Bone-forming cells that lay down new bone.

Osteoclasts
: Cells that resorb (break down) old bone.

Formation and resorption continue throughout life, a process called bone turnover; the coupled
resorption-then-formation cycle is called bone remodelling, and it dominates in the adult skeleton. The balance
between the two sets whether bone mass rises or falls, often pictured as deposits into and withdrawals from a
bank account. Through childhood and puberty, formation
outpaces resorption, so bone mass rises to its peak. Peak bone mass is mostly inherited; about 90% of it is
laid down by the end of adolescence, and the peak itself is reached in young adulthood, from the late teens
at the hip to the thirties at the spine. After the peak, resorption gradually exceeds formation, and bone
mass falls for the rest of life [@hereford2024peakBoneMass; @bailey1999saskatchewanAccrual;
@nof_weaver_2016_pbm_position]. This loss begins in young adulthood in both
sexes, so the modifiable factors matter across the whole life course, long before menopause as well as after
it [@riggs2008boneLossSites]. (The adolescent bone-building window, and the low energy availability that can
blunt it, are covered in the [*Childhood & Adolescence*](childhood-adolescence.qmd) chapter.)

<div data-island="bone-bank" data-src="/diagrams/bone-bank.yml"></div>

A higher peak bone mass postpones the age at which bone density falls to the osteoporosis threshold. In a
model, a 10% higher peak bone density delays the onset of osteoporosis by about 13 years, far more than a
later menopause or slower loss [@hernandez2003peakBmdModel]. The gain is measured in years of delay, not as a
percentage cut in fractures.

In women, the loss sharpens around the menopause. As oestrogen falls, the resorption signal RANKL rises and
shifts remodelling toward osteoclastic resorption [@eghbali2003rankl], and women lose roughly 7% of spine and
6% of femoral-neck bone mineral across the transition [@greendale2012swanBone]. The hormonal context, including
menopausal hormone therapy, is covered in the [*Menopause & Midlife Health*](menopause-midlife.qmd) chapter;
here we follow the diet.

Three nutrients act on bone, each in a different way (the nutrient biology is in the
[*Micronutrients, Hydration & Electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) and
[*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd) chapters):

| Nutrient | Role | How it acts on bone |
|---|---|---|
| Calcium | Mineral substrate | The mineral bone is built from |
| Vitamin D | Regulates calcium absorption | Its active form drives the intestinal absorption of calcium; it does not build bone directly |
| Protein | Organic matrix | About half of bone volume is a type-I collagen framework; protein also drives the growth factor IGF-1 and preserves the muscle that prevents falls |

Because vitamin D's active form drives calcium absorption, a shortfall means calcium passes through
unabsorbed, parathyroid hormone rises and mobilises calcium from bone, and bone mineral is lost
[@laird2010vitDbone].

(When failing kidneys can no longer balance calcium, phosphate and vitamin D, the result is CKD–mineral and
bone disease, which is recognised and referred; see the [*Chronic Kidney Disease*](chronic-kidney-disease.qmd)
chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does building a higher peak in youth protect against osteoporosis decades later?
After the peak in young adulthood, resorption gradually outpaces formation, so everyone's bone mass falls for the
rest of life. Starting from a higher peak means bone density takes longer to fall to the osteoporosis
threshold: in a model, a 10% higher peak delays onset by about 13 years, more than a later menopause or
slower loss. The gain is years of delay, not a percentage cut in fractures.
:::

## Modifiable factors in bone health {#sec-bone-levers}

### Calcium: requirements and bioavailability {#sec-bone-calcium}

Singapore's calcium requirements run across the life course, plus a raised need in pregnancy and lactation [@hpbRDACalcium]:

| Life stage | Calcium requirement (mg/day) |
|---|---|
| Adolescents (10–18) | 1,000 |
| Adults 19–50 | 800 |
| Adults 51 and over | 1,000 |
| Pregnancy and lactation | 1,000 |

Mean local intake is about 794 mg/day [@hpbNNS2010]. That is among the highest in Asia, where most countries
fall below 400–500 mg, but still under the requirement [@balkGlobalCalcium2017], and the gap widens with age:
about half of older Singaporeans fall short [@ye2023daha].

Absorption matters more than content. How much calcium a food delivers depends on its bioavailability, and
absorption varies enormously. The calcium in spinach is bound to oxalate, so only about 5% is absorbed, against
roughly a quarter to a third from milk [@odsCalcium]. Calcium-set tofu is absorbed about as well as milk, and
low-oxalate greens such as kai-lan and bok choy are absorbed better still [@weaverTofuMilk2002;
@weaverVegCalcium1999]. The spinach that looks calcium-rich on a label is therefore nearly useless for bone,
and the tofu beside it an excellent source (see the *Micronutrients, Hydration & Electrolytes* chapter for the
oxalate contrast).

![How much calcium a food delivers depends on how much is absorbed, not the amount it contains. Calcium in high-oxalate spinach is only about 5% absorbed; milk and calcium-set tofu sit around a quarter to a third; low-oxalate greens like kai-lan and bok choy are absorbed better still.](/figures/mechanisms/calcium-bioavailability.svg){#fig-calcium-bio width="82%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out (and eating in): the dairy-optional calcium plate
Dairy is optional in Singapore. Familiar foods close the gap, shown here with HPB's per-serving calcium
[@healthhubCalciumSG]:

- calcium-set tofu and tau kwa, as yong tau foo picks (tau kwa ~150 mg);
- ikan bilis and canned sardines eaten with the soft bones (~270 mg each);
- low-oxalate greens such as kai-lan, bok choy and chye sim (kai-lan ~195 mg);
- fortified soy milk (~500 mg), against ~380 mg for a glass of low-fat milk.

Small swaps stack up: tofu in the yong tau foo, milk in the kopi or teh, ikan bilis in the stock. Absorption
is best in doses under ~500 mg at a sitting, so spread calcium across the day [@odsCalcium].
:::

### Vitamin D: calcium absorption, and deficiency despite the sun {#sec-bone-vitd}

Vitamin D's active form, made in the skin from sunlight and finished in the liver and kidney, is required for
intestinal absorption of calcium [@laird2010vitDbone].

![Vitamin D from skin and diet is activated through the liver and kidney to its active form, which drives intestinal calcium absorption, keeping bone supplied. When vitamin D is low, calcium absorption falls, parathyroid hormone rises, and calcium is mobilised from bone, so the deficiency depletes bone mineral. Vitamin D does not build bone directly; it enables calcium to be absorbed.](/figures/mechanisms/vitamin-d-calcium-axis.svg){#fig-vitd-axis width="92%" fig-align="center"}

Despite the sun, vitamin D deficiency is common in equatorial Singapore: roughly 1 in 3 mid-life women are
deficient [@cheong2021vitDsg]. Behaviour and biology, not the climate, explain this. Each of the
following cuts skin synthesis of vitamin D [@nimitphong_2013_vitd_sea; @maclaughlin1985skinVitD]:

- indoor lifestyles;
- cosmetic sun avoidance;
- covering and veiling;
- darker skin pigmentation;
- age (in classic laboratory work, skin from people in their late seventies made less than half as much
  vitamin D as young skin, though newer work questions how large that effect is [@borecka2024skin7dhc]).

The burden is unequal: Indian and Malay women have several-fold higher odds of deficiency than Chinese women,
which makes deficiency an equity issue [@cheong2021vitDsg].

Common deficiency does not justify testing and dosing everyone. Few foods contain vitamin D naturally (oily
fish is the best) [@odsVitaminD], and the Endocrine Society guideline now suggests against routine testing, and
against empiric doses above the US Dietary Reference Intake in healthy adults under 75, while suggesting
empiric vitamin D for some groups, such as people aged 75 and over and pregnant women [@demay2024endoSocVitD]. HPB's own vitamin D reference
intake is a modest 2.5 µg (100 IU) because it assumes some sun exposure [@hpb_healthhub_rda]. Insufficiency by
the laboratory cut-off is common, but the response is to find and correct genuine shortfall in higher-risk
people (those who cover up, stay indoors, are older or are pregnant) rather than to blanket-dose the
population.

### Does protein leach calcium from bone? {#sec-bone-protein}

A widely held belief is that protein "leaches calcium from bone", an idea known as the **acid-ash
hypothesis**. The belief draws on the extra calcium that appears in the urine after a protein meal. The
evidence points the other way: that calcium comes from better intestinal absorption, not from dissolved
bone, and higher protein intake with adequate calcium tracks about 11% lower hip-fracture risk
[@groenendijk2019protein].

Protein's roles in bone explain the finding. It is the collagen matrix bone is built on, it drives the
bone-building growth factor IGF-1, and it maintains the muscle that keeps frail people from falling. (The
muscle–bone overlap is approached from the sarcopenia side in the
[*Undernutrition & Malnutrition*](undernutrition-malnutrition.qmd) and [*Healthy Ageing*](healthy-ageing.qmd)
chapters.) When an older patient worries that "meat is bad for my bones", the advice is the opposite of the
fear: eat enough protein, alongside enough calcium.

### Body weight and the whole pattern {#sec-bone-weight}

Adequate body weight is itself protective. A low BMI (20 versus 25) nearly doubles hip-fracture risk, largely
because low weight tracks lower bone density [@delaet2005bmiFracture]. Being underweight or having a low energy
intake is therefore a bone red flag, and the frailty of late life makes it common.

The whole dietary pattern matters more than any single nutrient: plenty of fruit and vegetables (supplying
potassium, magnesium and vitamin K), a reliable calcium source, enough protein and enough energy
[@iofNutritionProf]. (The overall pattern is set out in the
[*What a Healthy Diet Looks Like*](dietary-guidelines-patterns.qmd) chapter.)

::: {.callout-note}
## Mechanical loading: the strongest modifiable factor
Diet supports both building peak bone mass and slowing its later loss, but the strongest modifiable signal to
bone is mechanical loading, the weight-bearing and resistance exercise met in the *Menopause & Midlife Health*
chapter. In one small trial (101 women over 8 months), supervised high-intensity resistance and impact
training improved bone density more than a low-intensity home programme in postmenopausal women with low
bone mass, with only one minor adverse event [@watson2018liftmor]. Nutrition and loading are partners
(calcium is the substrate, loading is the signal to use it). When you advise a patient, name exercise as part
of the plan and leave the detailed prescription to physical-activity guidance; HPB's own public message pairs
a high-calcium diet with weight-bearing exercise [@hpbOsteoporosisAwareness2009].
:::

### Do salt, caffeine and cola harm bone? {#sec-bone-contested}

Some foods are blamed for weak bones on thin evidence. The solid dietary risks are low calcium, vitamin D or
protein, low body weight and heavy alcohol; smoking is a major non-dietary risk [@iofRiskFactors;
@ke2023alcoholFracture; @law1997smokingHipFracture]. Three popular claims are weaker than the headlines
suggest:

- Heavy salt raises urinary calcium, but its link to fracture is weak; the reason to cut salt is blood
  pressure [@teucher2008sodiumBone].
- Caffeine's tiny effect on bone is offset by the splash of milk in the coffee [@heaney2002caffeineBone].
- The cola–bone signal is observational and confounded by milk displacement; acid damage is not proven
  [@tucker2006colaBMD].

### Supplements: for deficiency, not for everyone {#sec-bone-supplements}

Calcium and vitamin D supplements together can cut fractures: one meta-analysis pooling trials in
community-dwelling and institutionalised adults found roughly 15% fewer fractures overall and 30% fewer hip
fractures, with the clearest effect in the two trials in institutional care [@weaver2016cavitd]. In
already-replete, community-dwelling older adults, however, large trials and pooled analyses find no fracture
benefit, and a small increase in kidney stones [@zhao2017cavitdNoBenefit; @leboff2022vitalFractures;
@uspstfCalcium2018]. The message is therefore food first: correct genuine deficiency, and reserve supplements
for real shortfall or high risk, rather than advising calcium and vitamin D for everyone over 50.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: spinach and calcium-set tofu both contain calcium. Why is the tofu the better source for bone?
What reaches bone is the calcium that is absorbed, not the amount the food contains. Spinach's calcium is
bound to oxalate, so only about 5% is absorbed, whereas calcium-set tofu is absorbed about as well as milk,
roughly a quarter to a third. The label's calcium content therefore overstates what spinach delivers.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a woman in her sixties who lives at home and is not deficient asks about calcium and vitamin D tablets. Why is the answer usually no?
Supplements cut fractures in people who are genuinely deficient or institutionalised, but in
already-replete, community-dwelling older adults large trials find no fracture benefit and a small increase
in kidney stones. She belongs to the second group, so the tablets would add a small risk without a fracture
benefit. Food first is the approach, with supplements reserved for genuine shortfall or high risk.
:::

## The joints {#sec-bone-joints}

::: {.spectrum}
[Evidence for joint treatments and claims]{.tree-title}

- Glucosamine and chondroitin for osteoarthritis: no better than placebo in the major independent trials
- Cherries for gout: an observational signal only
- Omega-3 fish oil in rheumatoid arthritis: a modest adjunct
- The effective treatments: about 10% weight loss in knee osteoarthritis; a urate-lowering drug to target in gout

[No proven benefit]{.spectrum-end} [Proven benefit]{.spectrum-end}
:::

### Osteoarthritis: weight loss, not supplements {#sec-bone-oa}

Osteoarthritis, the commonest arthritis and a very high local burden, is where the most-asked supplement
question lands, and the answer has two parts.

The first is that the measure that works is weight loss (with activity). Obesity is the leading modifiable risk,
acting through both the mechanical load on the joint and the low-grade inflammation of adipose tissue
[@shumnalieva2023obesityoa]. In the IDEA trial, a diet-plus-exercise programme that lost about 10% of body
weight improved pain and function while measurably lowering both knee load and inflammation, and more loss
gave more benefit [@messier2013idea; @messier2018morebetter].

The second is that the supplements do not work. Glucosamine and chondroitin, the best-selling joint
supplements, are no better than placebo for pain or joint structure in the major independent trials
[@clegg2006gait; @wandel2010nma]. The major guidelines all advise against them: those of the American
College of Rheumatology (ACR), the Osteoarthritis Research Society International (OARSI), the National
Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and Singapore's Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE)
[@kolasinski2020acr; @bannuru2019oarsi; @nice2022ng226; @aceKneeOA2026]. The one dissenting voice, the
European ESCEO group (a musculoskeletal-disease society), makes a case for a specific patented formulation
[@bruyere2018esceo]. It remains a minority position: the ACR panel noted that pharmaceutical-grade
preparations have been studied, flagged discrepancies between industry-sponsored and publicly funded trials,
and still advised strongly against glucosamine [@kolasinski2020acr].
Other popular pills (vitamin D, collagen, curcumin) fare no better, with negative or very-low-quality evidence
in osteoarthritis [@mcalindon2013vitd; @lin2023collagenoa].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Glucosamine: professional guidance versus consumer messaging
Glucosamine shows how consumer messaging can outrun the evidence. Singapore's professional guidance (ACE)
states that glucosamine and chondroitin "may add cost without established clinical benefit" for knee
osteoarthritis, yet the government consumer portal (HealthHub) still frames glucosamine positively, as
something that "may help provide relief" [@aceKneeOA2026; @healthhubGlucosamine]. The do-no-harm point is
subtle: these supplements are physically fairly safe, so the harm is not toxicity but **cost, false
reassurance, and spending on an ineffective pill instead of the intervention that works** (losing weight and
staying active). When a patient asks "should I take glucosamine?", the money is better spent on the measures
that work.
:::

### Gout: diet and urate-lowering treatment {#sec-bone-gout}

Gout is the one joint condition where particular foods matter, if only modestly, and it is misunderstood at
both ends. Patients are often told it is "their fault for eating too much seafood" and respond by cutting
food drastically; both the blame and the over-restriction are wrong.

Gout is a metabolic disease of **urate** handling (urate is uric acid, whose crystals inflame the joint). Diet
nudges urate in both directions, but only modestly [@choi2004purine; @choi2004alcohol; @choi2008fructose;
@choi2007coffee]:

- red and organ meat and some seafood raise it, because they are rich in **purines**, which are metabolised to urate (purine-rich vegetables and total protein, however, are not the problem at all);
- alcohol, especially beer, raises it;
- fructose and sugary drinks raise it;
- low-fat dairy and coffee lower it.


The ACR gout guideline grades these dietary limits as only conditional, on low-quality evidence, and the
popular remedies fare no better: cherries are linked to fewer flares only in observational data, and vitamin C
does not meaningfully lower urate [@fitzgerald2020goutacr; @zhang2012cherry; @stamp2013vitc].

The effective treatment is a urate-lowering drug (allopurinol) titrated to a target blood urate level
[@fitzgerald2020goutacr]. Singapore's own data show that the real problem is under-treatment: most local gout
patients never reach that target [@lee2023sggout; @oka2023goutcontrol].

When you counsel a patient with gout, the message runs: "It is not your fault. Don't starve yourself of
protein and vegetables, cut the beer and sugary drinks if you like, and take the medication to target."
(Obesity is linked to a higher risk of gout, and the ACR guideline conditionally recommends weight loss for
patients with gout who are overweight [@fitzgerald2020goutacr]; obesity itself is covered in the
[*Obesity & Metabolic Syndrome*](obesity-metabolic-syndrome.qmd) chapter.)

### Rheumatoid arthritis: nutrition as an adjunct {#sec-bone-ra}

**Rheumatoid arthritis**, an autoimmune joint disease managed with disease-modifying drugs, is different
again: nutrition is only a modest adjunct. Omega-3 fish oil can ease symptoms and spare some
anti-inflammatory medication, and a Mediterranean pattern may help a little, but neither substitutes for the
drugs [@fraenkel2021raacr; @goldberg2007omega3jointpain; @proudman2015fishoilra; @papandreou2023madeira].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does losing about 10% of body weight help a painful knee when glucosamine does not?
Obesity loads the joint mechanically and adds the low-grade inflammation of adipose tissue. In the IDEA
trial, losing about 10% of body weight improved pain and function while lowering both knee load and
inflammation, with more loss giving more benefit. In the major independent trials, glucosamine and
chondroitin were no better than placebo for pain or joint structure, which is why the major guidelines advise
against them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient with gout plans to cut out meat, seafood and vegetables entirely. Why is that the wrong focus?
Diet nudges urate only modestly: beer, sugary drinks and red and organ meat raise it, but purine-rich
vegetables and total protein are not the problem. The effective treatment is a urate-lowering drug titrated to
a target urate level, and in Singapore most patients never reach that target. Drastic restriction misses the
treatment that works.
:::

## Bones and joints: what actually helps? {#sec-bone-close}

Bone and the joints call for almost opposite answers. For bone, the modifiable factors are real and correctable:

- a high peak bone mass built in youth, then slower bone loss across adulthood;
- a well-absorbed calcium source (dairy optional), with enough vitamin D, protein and energy;
- weight-bearing exercise;
- correction of genuine deficiency without medicalising everyone, and referral for a bone-density scan
  (case-finding is set out in [The Singapore picture](#sec-bone-singapore)).

For the joints, the answer is usually less about a pill:

- weight loss and activity for a worn knee;
- urate-lowering treatment to target for gout, without blaming the seafood;
- no glucosamine, the supplement the guidelines advise against.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-bone-singapore}

**Two local facts overturn imported assumptions.** Vitamin D deficiency is common in a sunny country, driven
by behaviour and pigmentation and unequal across ethnic groups (see [vitamin D](#sec-bone-vitd) above)
[@cheong2021vitDsg]. Average calcium intake (~794 mg/day) falls short, with about half of older adults below
the requirement (see [calcium](#sec-bone-calcium) above) [@ye2023daha]. The imported assumptions (that a
sunny country has little vitamin D deficiency, and that calcium means dairy) therefore fail here, which is why
a dairy-optional, food-first calcium list matters.

**Hip-fracture rates are falling, but the count is rising.** Singapore's hip-fracture *rates* have fallen
since 2000 (and continued to fall to 2022), yet absolute *cases* keep rising with the ageing population, and
osteoporotic fractures are projected to climb further by 2035 [@yong2019hipfracSG; @aceOsteoporosis2025;
@chandran2019burdenSG]. Fractures are about twice as common in women as in men, and Chinese Singaporeans
carry the highest ethnic risk [@yong2019hipfracSG]. A hip fracture also carries high mortality: about double
the background rate in women, and higher in men [@yong2020mortalitySG].

**National guidance sets case-finding and treatment.** HPB's public message pairs two measures, a
high-calcium diet and weight-bearing exercise [@hpbOsteoporosisAwareness2009]. Four terms describe
case-finding and diagnosis:

OSTA
: An Asian screen, based on age and weight, that flags who needs a bone scan [@koh2001osta].

FRAX
: A tool that estimates 10-year fracture probability, with Singapore-calibrated models [@fraxSingapore].

T-score
: Bone density on a DXA scan (the low-dose X-ray scan met in the [*Energy Balance*](energy-balance.qmd)
  chapter), expressed in standard deviations from the young-adult peak.

Fragility fracture
: A break from a fall from standing height or less.

A T-score of −2.5 or below, or any fragility fracture, defines osteoporosis [@aceOsteoporosis2018]. Drug
treatment and menopausal hormone decisions are specialist, guided by the national ACE guidance and the 2025
Singapore consensus; at this level they are signposted, not managed
[@aceOsteoporosis2025; @gani2025osteoconsensusSG].

::: {.callout-important}
## Recognise and refer, for bone and joints alike
For bone, recognise the modifiable nutrient factors (calcium, vitamin D, protein, energy), correct genuine
deficiency without blanket-supplementing, and refer using OSTA, FRAX and DXA. For the joints, recognise that
the effective measures are weight loss and activity for osteoarthritis and a urate-lowering drug to target
for gout, and that the best-selling joint supplement does not work. The osteoporosis drugs and hormone
therapy, the allopurinol titration and the arthritis disease-modifying drugs are all **specialist: named and
referred, never prescribed at this level** [@aceOsteoporosis2018; @kolasinski2020acr; @fitzgerald2020goutacr].
:::

Madam Lim, 58 and three years past menopause, is lactose-intolerant, mostly indoors and covered up, with a
BMI of 19 and no fracture yet. She has read that everyone her age should take calcium and vitamin D tablets,
and wonders whether she needs a bone medicine. Your choices branch the case.

## Practise: Mr Tan and the glucosamine question {#sec-bone-case-tan}

Mr Tan, 62, is overweight (BMI 29), and his knees ache on the stairs, with no red flags. He has seen
glucosamine advertised and wants to know whether it will rebuild his cartilage. Your choices branch the case.

<div data-island="case" data-src="/cases/mr-tan-joint.case.yml"></div>
